issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For an adult male sexual assault survivor, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the selected items and formulation. The other triggers (related news, motorcycle noise) plausibly cue intrusive memory reactivation, and the memory items are all intrusion/emotion based. 'Being around children' implies a distinct trauma meaning or developmental context that is not reflected anywhere in Memory, Threat, Negative Appraisals, or Maladaptive Strategies. Given the formulation is dominated by Triggers ↔ Memory links, this trigger stands out as insufficiently supported by the accompanying memory content and is the one item most likely to be incoherent.

vignette:
Kai, a forty-eight-year-old roofer of Pacific Islander descent, had always taken pride in his physical strength and the steady rhythm of his work-hoisting bundles of shingles, balancing on pitched roofs under the heavy sun. That sense of competence was shattered three years ago, late on a Friday afternoon, when he stayed behind to finish a small repair at a residential site. A younger coworker, a man Kai had trusted, approached him near the tool trailer. The man reeked of alcohol-cheap whiskey, familiar from countless other after-work beers. Before Kai fully understood what was happening, the coworker shoved him against the trailer, overpowered him, and sexually assaulted him while a motorcycle roared past on the street below, its engine popping and stuttering. Kai froze, disbelieving, until it was over. He told no one. He washed himself off in the client's backyard hose, drove home, and sat in the dark garage for an hour, trying to convince himself it hadn't happened.

Over the following weeks, Kai's world began to narrow in ways he couldn't name at first. The motorcycle noise that had been an ordinary part of his day-kids joyriding, delivery bikes-now made his chest lock and his breath go shallow. More than once he stopped his truck at an intersection, hands white on the wheel, because a bike idled two cars ahead. He also found himself avoiding the break room at the supply yard whenever he caught the whiff of alcohol on someone's breath; the smell of it from a grocery aisle could send him walking out of the store without his cart. And when the local news ran a segment about a workplace sexual assault case in another state, Kai switched off the television so fast that his wife Leilani asked if he was ill. He told her he was just tired.

His memories of the assault had an unnerving vividness. Ordinary recollections of other days-lunch with Leilani, a roofing job he'd finished-felt faded and flat in comparison, while the image of the trailer's rusted hitch and the feel of gravel against his cheek rose up with a presence that seemed more real than his actual present. Sometimes, without any picture at all, Kai would be seized by a wave of pure emotional intensity-shame, helplessness, fear-that left him trembling in the middle of a conversation or standing still on a roof, gripping his hammer. Worst of all were the moments when remembering brought not fear but a crushing, overwhelming grief, a sorrow that felt as if something irreplaceable had been stolen from him. He couldn't explain it, even to himself.

To cope, Kai developed a set of habits that, at first, felt like sensible self-protection. He began to avoid any physical exertion that pushed his body into stress-refusing to carry the heaviest bundles of shingles, declining overtime that required extra lifting, even pulling out of the weekend basketball games he had played for years. On the job he made excuses, saying his back was acting up, and his foreman, though skeptical, let it slide. At home, he started controlling his eating with strict, almost ritualistic precision-eating the same small meals at the same times, never snacking, never allowing himself to feel out of control around food. And he filled every empty hour with busyness: staying late to clean tools, taking on odd projects at home, volunteering to help relatives move furniture. If he kept moving, he reasoned, the past couldn't catch up.

The consequences accumulated quietly. Leilani noticed that he no longer sat still with her in the evenings; he was always pacing, doing something, and when she tried to talk he'd say he was too busy. Their conversations grew thinner. At work, his avoidance of physical stress made him less reliable; his crew leader started giving the more demanding jobs to younger roofers, and Kai felt a slow erosion of his identity as a capable workman. He began to feel like a stranger in his own life, hollowed out by a secret he could not speak and a grief he could not name.

What finally brought Kai to a clinic was an incident three weeks ago. He was at a traffic light when a motorcycle pulled up beside him, the rider revving the engine; the sound, the smell of exhaust, and a random whiff of alcohol from a nearby pedestrian all hit him at once. He had a full panic reaction-pounding heart, sweating, a sense that he was back at that trailer-and he drove straight home and sat in the garage again, just as he had on that first night. Leilani found him there. This time, he didn't lie. He told her something bad had happened, and she listened without pressing. She found him a therapist who specialized in trauma. Kai is terrified that talking about it will make the memories more real, more permanent. But more than that, he is hoping-though he would not say it aloud-that somewhere in that talk there might be a way to feel like himself again, to stop carrying the event as a constant, invisible weight.
